title: Laravel scheduled tasks not running: the cron entry most people forget
excerpt: Laravel's scheduler needs exactly one cron entry on the server, and without it every schedule() definition is dead code. Set it up correctly, run it as the right user, and verify tasks actually fire.
content:
You define tasks in routes/console.php or App\Console\Kernel, everything works with php artisan schedule:run by hand - and in production nothing ever runs. The cause is almost always the same: the scheduler is not a daemon. It is a command that something else must trigger every minute, and that something is a single cron entry that deploys routinely forget.

The one cron entry

Laravel's scheduler needs exactly one line in cron, running every minute:

* * * * * cd /var/www/app && php artisan schedule:run >> /dev/null 2>&1

Each minute, schedule:run evaluates your schedule and fires whatever is due. No cron entry, no scheduled tasks - regardless of how perfect the schedule definitions are. On newer Laravel versions you can also verify from the framework's side: php artisan schedule:list shows every defined task and its next due time.

Run it as the right user

The most common broken setup is the entry in root's crontab. Root-run workers create log and cache files in storage/ owned by root, and the next web request throws Permission denied. Install the entry in the crontab of the user that runs PHP-FPM, usually www-data:

sudo crontab -e -u www-data

If your deploys run as a separate user, pick that user consistently for cron, workers and deploys, and keep group ownership of storage/ correct.

Cron's environment is not yours

Cron runs with a minimal PATH and no loaded profile. php artisan schedule:run can fail with "command not found" when php is not on cron's PATH, or load the wrong PHP version on multi-version servers. Use the absolute binary:

* * * * * cd /var/www/app && /usr/bin/php8.3 artisan schedule:run >> /dev/null 2>&1

While debugging, drop the >> /dev/null 2>&1 redirect so failures mail you or land in the syslog: grep CRON /var/log/syslog.

Prove tasks actually fire

Three quick checks:

php artisan schedule:list          # what exists and when it is next due
php artisan schedule:test          # interactive dry-run of due tasks
grep CRON /var/log/syslog | tail   # cron is invoking the entry at all

Inside the schedule, add observability to the tasks that matter:

Schedule::command('reports:send')->daily()
    ->emailOutputOnFailure('ops@example.com')
    ->appendOutputTo(storage_path('logs/scheduler.log'));

Multi-server and overlap traps

On more than one server the cron entry runs on each of them, so every task fires once per server. Add ->onOneServer() (needs a shared cache like Redis) to elect a single runner. For long tasks that could outlive their interval, ->withoutOverlapping() prevents a slow run from stacking on top of itself. Forgetting withoutOverlapping is how a daily report that starts taking 25 hours brings a server down a month later.

Summary

The scheduler is one cron line: every minute, as the PHP-FPM user, with an absolute PHP path. Verify with schedule:list and the syslog, add output logging to important tasks, and use onOneServer() and withoutOverlapping() as soon as the app grows. Write the cron entry into your provisioning script - the day you rebuild the server is the day it gets forgotten again.
author: Stefan Bogdanescu
